draw.question: After the power returns and you check the freezer, which food can be safely refrozen?

draw.question: What is the maximum length of power outage this guide prepares an ordinary household for?

draw.question: For how long does refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remain usable at room temperature, and who should you confirm the rule with?

F1 (intro) This guide explains how to prepare an ordinary household to manage safely and comfortably through a power outage lasting up to seventy-two hours. [scope: up to 72 hours]
F2 (intro) It is written for a temperate climate and assumes no backup generator. [temperate; no generator]
F3 (intro) Work through the sections in order; the earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most. [work in order]
F4 (Water) Store four litres of water per person per day, which means twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours. [4 L/person/day = 12 L/72h]
F5 (Water) Half of that allowance is for drinking, and the other half covers cooking and basic hygiene. [half drink / half cook+hygiene]
F6 (Water) Store the water in food-grade containers, keep the containers out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months. [food-grade; no sunlight; replace 6 months]
F7 (Water) If a storm is forecast and you have advance warning, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking. [fill bathtub; flush/wash not drink]
F8 (Food) Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food sufficient for three days. [3 days non-perishable]
F9 (Food) Good choices are canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk. [item list]
F10 (Food) Choose foods that require no cooking, and make sure you own a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless. [no-cook; manual can opener]
F11 (Food) Eat the perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the food from the freezer, and only then open the emergency shelf. [order: fridge, freezer, shelf]
F12 (Fridge/freezer) An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours. [~4 h fridge]
F13 (Fridge/freezer) A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours, but a half-full freezer holds it for only about twenty-four hours, so it is worth keeping the freezer consolidated and full, even if some of the space is taken up by containers of frozen water. [~48 h full / ~24 h half]
F14 (Fridge/freezer) Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a note to each door as a reminder. [doors closed; tape note each door]
F15 (Fridge/freezer) Any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius should be discarded; when in doubt, throw it out. [>2 h above 4 C discard]
F16 (Light) Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light source, and avoid candles entirely, since candles are a leading cause of house fires during outages. [battery LED lanterns/headlamps; no candles]
F17 (Light) Store at least one light per person, plus two spare sets of batteries for each light. [1 light/person + 2 spare battery sets/light]
F18 (Light) Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, and place them where they can be found in the dark. [1 headlamp/bed; 1 lantern kitchen]
F19 (Heat/safety) Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window, because each of these produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal. [no combustion indoors; CO odourless/fatal]
F20 (Heat/safety) Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep. [>=1 CO alarm per sleeping floor]
F21 (Heat/safety) In cold weather, choose one small room on a south-facing side of the home, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater. [one small south-facing room; layers/blankets]
F22 (Heat/safety) If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home. [below 10 C relocate]
F23 (Comms) Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and know the frequency of your local emergency station before the outage begins. [radio; know station frequency]
F24 (Comms) Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times. [20,000 mAh ~4 recharges]
F25 (Comms) Put your phone in low-power mode at the start of the outage, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every member of the household will text, because text messages get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls. [low-power mode; one out-of-area text contact]
F26 (Medical) Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, and rotate the medications so they stay in date. [first-aid kit; 7-day meds; rotate]
F27 (Medical) Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist before an emergency happens. [insulin 28 days room temp; confirm pharmacist]
F28 (Medical) Write down the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book. [pharmacy/doctor/poison-control on paper]
F29 (Power returns) Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise. [wait 5 minutes]
F30 (Power returns) Check the freezer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen. [ice crystals -> refreeze]
F31 (Power returns) Restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries. [restock within 1 week; start water/batteries]
F32 (Power returns) Finally, write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one of those gaps before the next outage arrives. [one-page note; fix >=1 gap]
